facts.impl: INFERENCE: a token-budget lever may exist for capping quota in long unattended runs. Its semantics are in a page outside this chunk.

facts.claim: Explicitly setting effort to the model's default is identical to omitting it.
facts.impl: Pinning --effort medium on Opus 5.5 is behavior-neutral and guards against later default changes.

facts.claim: Top-level effort needs no beta header on any supported model; only per-message effort is beta.
On Opus 5, thinking can be disabled only at high effort or below; at xhigh/max, thinking:disabled returns 400. On Opus 5.5 it returns 400 at every level.
facts.impl: Any harness sending thinking:disabled breaks on an Opus 5.5 id swap, which is one of the migration's breaking changes.

facts.claim: Sonnet 4.6 defaults to high, but the recommended default is medium for agentic coding and tool-heavy workflows; set effort explicitly to avoid unexpected latency.
Opus 4.5 is the only extended-thinking-only model supporting effort, and there effort works alongside budget_tokens.
An effort-only system message may appear anywhere in messages, including as the first entry; the placement rules for mid-conversation system messages don't apply.
On Opus 4.7, if effort must stay low for latency, a targeted prompt line can compensate for shallow reasoning.
The effort parameter is available on Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Bedrock, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry, and is ZDR-eligible except for Covered Models.
The explore-broadly instruction tells the model to act on what it finds, so untrusted content must be kept out of the searched records, which makes it an injection-exposure trade-off.
facts.impl: Do not add the explore-first line to web-research agents that ingest untrusted pages.

facts.claim: With the unattended early-stop addition, the model's status notes move into progress-update blocks (empty at default display), and the operator must keep their own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions.
facts.impl: Combining this addition with default display makes a working session look silent to text-keyed liveness detectors.

facts.claim: Migrating from Opus 5 involves four breaking API changes, covered in the migration guide.
The biology classifier (new vs Opus 5) can block life-sciences work; the remedy is the Life Sciences Verification Program.
Opus 5.5 is better at position-dependent visual meaning: flowchart arrow endpoints, diffs between diagram versions, and exact start/end times in calendar screenshots.
Opus 5.5's reports on agentic work, both updates while working and the final summary, state plainly what it did, found, and needs.
Opus 5.5 is positioned as performing at Fable 5.1's level on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: Opus 5.5 is the candidate to replace Opus 5 as the fleet default and to take over most Fable 5.1 escalations.

facts.claim: The 40% cost cut comes from both a lower per-token price and fewer tokens per task. Cache reads are $0.20/M, 60% below Opus 5, and the vendor says cache reads make up most agentic and coding cost.
facts.n: input $4 vs $5; output $20 vs $25; cache reads $0.20 vs $0.50; cache writes $5 vs $6.25; 40% lower cost at default settings
facts.impl: INFERENCE: quota is probably tied to compute/tokens, not list price, so the token cut per task is the part likely to carry over to weekly plan quota. That carry-over is unverified.

facts.claim: Opus 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: shorter wall-clock per wave for leads and teammates, even at the same effort.

facts.claim: Five-hour usage limits are going up on Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans, and subscribers get a rate-limit reset they can save and use when they choose. No size is given, and weekly limits are not mentioned.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: the saveable reset on each of our 4 Max accounts is a one-time buffer to spend on a real wall. The binding weekly cap is not stated to change, so we have to measure it.

facts.claim: Fast mode for Opus 5.5 runs up to 2.5x faster and costs $8/$40 per million input/output tokens, 2x standard. The announcement says it is available in Claude Code and the Claude Platform. The What's new doc says it is a research preview, on the Claude API only.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: if quota follows price, fast mode likely burns quota about 2x per token. Keep it off by default and use it only where a human is waiting on the result.

facts.models: Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol
facts.claim: Headline benchmark table. Opus 5.5 leads Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 on every row. GPT-6 Astra beats Opus 5.5 on AutomationBench and Terminal-Bench-Science.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: this chunk has no benchmark where Fable 5.1 at its best beats Opus 5.5 at its best, so any Fable escalation must rest on evidence from outside this source.

facts.claim: Table caption: Opus 5.5 results use max effort, except Terminal-Bench 4.0, which is reported at xhigh. Runs had production safeguards on. When they intervened, Opus 4.8 did the cybersecurity tasks and Opus 5 did the biology and frontier-LLM-development tasks.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: work that looks like frontier LLM development, such as model/eval infrastructure, may be silently answered by Opus 5 rather than Opus 5.5. Watch for quality drops on that kind of work. [VERIFIER: 'Silently' is not supported. The announcement (L564) says the fallbacks happen 'transparently', and whatsnew L99 says a declined request returns stop_reason 'refusal' with a stop_details category, and fallback is configured. The caption describes the benchmark setup. It does not say production traffic about model/eval infrastructure is routed to Opus 5, and there is no production 'frontier LLM development' category in the whatsnew/migration category list (cyber, bio, reasoning_extraction).]

facts.claim: Benchmark footnotes. Terminal-Bench 4.0 standard error is ±2.6 pts for Opus 5.5 and ±1.6–2 for other Claude models, with Opus 5 reproduced at 52.3% against a 51.8% leaderboard (Claude Code harness, 5 trials/task). Zapier ran AutomationBench without fallback models, so safeguard interventions counted as failures. Terminal-Bench-Science standard error is ±3.5–5 pts.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: at ±2.6 pts, per-effort differences of 1–2 pts on TB4, such as xhigh 66.4 vs max 64.8, are within noise.

facts.ref: announce.html chart tuskchartterminalbench (embedded data); announce.txt L123
facts.models: Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol
facts.claim: Terminal-Bench 4.0 cost vs accuracy by effort (cost per attempt, USD). Opus 5.5 peaks at xhigh and max scores lower than xhigh. Medium Opus 5.5 beats max Opus 5 and max Fable 5.1 at a fraction of the cost.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: for terminal-heavy coding teammates, high gets ~97% of the peak score for ~53% of xhigh's cost. max is dominated by xhigh, so never use max here.

facts.models: Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol
facts.claim: FrontierCode v1.1 cost vs accuracy by effort is non-monotone. Opus 5.5 scores best at medium, and xhigh scores worst after low. Fable 5.1 scores best at low. Opus 5 scores best at medium.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: for mergeable-PR code writing, going above medium buys nothing and costs 1.4–7.7x. Default code-writing teammates to Opus 5.5 at medium. [VERIFIER: Overreach from one benchmark. The other coding chart in the same source (CursorBench, F11) shows high +3.5 over medium, and TB4 (F9) shows high +6.6 over medium. 'Going above medium buys nothing' holds only for FrontierCode, and the FrontierCode differences (≈0.6–3 pts) are unreported-SE noise.]

facts.claim: CursorBench 4.0 cost vs accuracy by effort. Opus 5.5 at medium (52.5) beats Fable 5.1 at max (51.8) and Opus 5 at max (46.6). Opus 5.5 high and xhigh both score 56.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: for ambiguous multi-file coding, high is the knee: +3.5 pts over medium for 1.37x cost. xhigh adds nothing over high, and max adds +1.8 for ~3.4x the cost of high.

facts.ref: announce.html chart tuskchartgdpval; announce.txt L248, L270
facts.models: Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol
facts.claim: GDPval-AA v2.1 knowledge-work Elo vs estimated cost by effort. Opus 5.5 rises steeply from low to xhigh. Opus 5.5 at low has the lowest Elo of any plotted point.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: avoid low for knowledge work and synthesis (research writeups, plans). Opus 5.5 at high (1692) beats Fable 5.1 at max (1735 is higher, but costs ~6x more) only narrowly on Elo per dollar; use high as the baseline and xhigh for final deliverables. [VERIFIER: The implication contradicts itself. It says Opus 5.5 high (1692) 'beats' Fable 5.1 max (1735) and then concedes 1735 is higher. On Elo, Opus 5.5 high trails Fable max by 43, at ~1/6.2 the cost (1.54 vs 9.59). The 'avoid low' and 'xhigh for deliverables' parts are supported.]

facts.models: Opus 5.5, Opus 5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol
facts.claim: AutomationBench (Zapier business workflows) cost vs accuracy by effort. Opus 5.5 improves monotonically and beats Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol at every effort level. GPT-6 Astra at max (41.4) edges Opus 5.5 at max (40). No Fable 5.1 series is plotted.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: for multi-app tool workflows, cost across efforts is compressed (only 2.7x from low to max), so max is cheap relative to its +11.4 pt gain over medium.

facts.claim: WANDR (Claude runs with a 980k-token task budget; x-axis is cost per ATTEMPT). Opus 5.5 at low collapses to 31.2. Fable 5.1 low (63.3) beats Opus 5.5 medium (62.8). Opus 5.5 high (67.3, $16.88) beats Fable 5.1 low/med/high (63.3–66.7) and costs less than any Fable point, but trails Fable xhigh (67.7) and max (68.7). Only Opus 5.5 xhigh (71.3, $29.06) and max (72.3, $37.92) beat every Fable point, and they cost more than Fable low ($23.25) and med ($27.41).
facts.impl: INFERENCE: never run breadth-first web-research fan-outs at low. Use high or xhigh on Opus 5.5 rather than escalating to Fable 5.1.

facts.claim: At low effort, Fable 5.1 beats Opus 5.5 on every benchmark with a low point for both, but always at a higher cost. On FrontierCode, Fable 5.1 at low also beats Opus 5.5 at xhigh.
facts.n: low vs low — TB4 40.2 vs 38.5; FrontierCode 52.8 vs 47.3; CursorBench 45.1 vs 43.7; GDPval 1450 vs 1224; WANDR 63.3 vs 31.2. FrontierCode: Fable low 52.8 > Opus5.5 xhigh 51.42
facts.impl: INFERENCE: low-effort Opus 5.5 degrades more than low-effort Fable 5.1. Low is safe for Opus 5.5 only on mechanical tasks, not on research or open-ended work.

facts.claim: The vendor calls benchmark margins a less reliable guide at this capability level and says that in its own use the Opus 5.5–Fable 5.1 gap is narrower than the scores suggest.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: do not read the large table margins as proof that Fable 5.1 is obsolete. Keep a small Fable lane for framing-class holes.

facts.claim: Vendor-reported internal test: translating HAProxy from C to Rust. Both models passed nearly all regression tests, but Opus 5.5 took 9.5 hours versus 12 for Fable 5.1, at 51% less cost.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: for long-horizon unattended code translation or migration, Opus 5.5 reaches the same outcome as Fable 5.1 faster and for about half the cost.

facts.claim: Vendor-reported customer anecdote: an early tester audited and fixed a 200,000-line codebase in under 3 hours, where Opus 5 took over 20 hours and 2.5x the tokens. Another tester did a 680,000-line migration in under a day.
facts.n: <3 h vs >20 h; 2.5x tokens; 680k lines <1 day
facts.impl: INFERENCE: the biggest token savings may show up in long sprawling audits and migrations, which are our long-horizon unattended runs.

facts.claim: Internal perf-optimization test: asked to cut load times across every page of a web app, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times. Opus 5 made smaller improvements that also changed the app's behavior.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: less behavior-altering overreach during optimization, which matters for unattended edit agents.

facts.claim: Internal research test: write a report from a web copy where the source was hard to find, with a grader checking every figure and quote. 16 of Opus 5.5's 18 reports, across effort settings, cleared the bar. Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 cleared it in none of their attempts.
facts.impl: INFERENCE: Opus 5.5 fabricates figures and quotes less in research synthesis, a strong reason to move research subagents off Fable 5.1 and Opus 5. The effort breakdown of the 16/18 is not given. [VERIFIER: 'Strong reason' overreaches. gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: this is an adversarial prompt-injection set built to provoke harmful actions. Do not use it as the benign coding reroute rate.

gapFacts.claim: Gray Swan fallbacks concentrated in coding: 46% of Opus 5.5's coding rollouts fell back, versus 2% in tool use and under 1% in computer use. None of the 1,310 fallback-served rollouts led to a successful attack.
gapFacts.n: coding 46%; tool use 2%; computer use <1%; 0 of 1,310 fallback rollouts attacked successfully
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: coding scenarios with injected exfiltration or system-compromise content trip the cyber classifier heavily. A teammate reading hostile repo content may be served by Opus 4.8 far more often than the benign 2.5-3.9%.

gapFacts.claim: In Shade adaptive coding, 64% of Opus 5.5's valid-response requests were served by Opus 4.8, versus 60% for Fable 5.1 and 14% for Opus 5 with thinking.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: under adversarial coding pressure the stricter Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 classifiers reroute about 4.5x more than Opus 5's. Code that looks attack-shaped loses the Opus 5.5 brain most of the time.

gapFacts.claim: In Shade coding, attack success on fallback-served requests was 85.73%. None of the 2,872 requests Opus 5.5 answered directly were susceptible, so the overall ASR (54.61%) is driven entirely by the fallback.
gapFacts.n: fallback ASR 85.73%; direct 0/2,872; overall 54.61% (Fable 5.1 51.93%, Opus 5 88.92%, Sonnet 5 19.47%)
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the injection weakness of Opus 5.5 coding agents is the Opus 4.8 fallback. Security-audit sessions over untrusted code inherit Opus 4.8's susceptibility, and auto-mode probes are the mitigation that matters.

gapFacts.claim: With prompt-injection probes enabled, Opus 5.5's Shade coding ASR drops to 11.13% (Fable 5.1 8.70%, Opus 5 19.53%, Sonnet 5 15.76%). All successful attacks still came from fallback-served requests.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: keep auto mode / injection probes on for any agent reading untrusted content. Without them the rerouted share is badly exposed.

gapFacts.claim: Anthropic says the Opus 4.8 fallback reduces injection robustness and has since hardened Opus 4.8's safeguards. Fable 5.1's with-probes ASR fell from 12.80% to 8.70%.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the fallback weakness is known and partly mitigated. It is still the weakest link for review/audit workloads over hostile inputs.

gapFacts.claim: In Shade computer use only 6% of Opus 5.5's requests were served by Opus 4.8, and none were compromised. In browser use a fallback happened in 8% of attempts, and the one successful attack was executed by Opus 4.8.
gapFacts.n: computer use 6%; browser 8%; browser ASR without safeguards 0.09%, 0 with auto mode
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: outside coding, fallback shares are single-digit even under attack. The coding surface is the one where rerouting dominates.

gapFacts.models: Opus 5.5 bare vs + safety measures (Opus 5 in brackets)
gapFacts.claim: Fallback raises automated-audit misuse scores slightly, because the weaker fallback models are sometimes less strict about refusing misuse.
gapFacts.n: approx.: cyberoffense 1.01 -> 1.11 (Opus 5 1.02); cooperation with human misuse 1.34 -> 1.71 (1.62); targeted violence 1.04 -> 1.12 (1.12); bio 1.00 -> 1.01; chem 1.00 -> 1.03; explosives 1.01 -> 1.03
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the rerouted share behaves more like Opus 4.8/Opus 5 on misuse compliance. For adversarial verifiers of security findings, a rerouted turn is a weaker and laxer judge. [VERIFIER: The metrics measure compliance with harmful requests. They say nothing about judging or verification quality. 'A weaker and laxer judge' of security findings is not supported by this figure. Note also that explosives rises (1.01→1.03) although p.13 says that classifier has no fallback, so the small deltas are within the error bars.]

gapFacts.claim: A router or fallback moving a conversation off Opus 5.5 runs those turns without Opus 5.5's thinking blocks (only Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 read them).
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: a mid-session reroute also loses the prior reasoning context. In long lead or audit sessions a fallback turn is weaker model plus amnesia about earlier thinking.

gapFacts.claim: A classifier decline returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal' and stop_details naming the category. Server-side fallback (fallbacks: 'default', beta) retries on the model Anthropic recommends for that category.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the category is machine-readable, so our fleet could count its own cyber/bio/reasoning_extraction reroutes per use case instead of guessing from vendor benchmarks.

gapFacts.claim: Without extra safeguards, Opus 5.5 in Claude Code assisted with dual-use and benign cyber requests 99.8% of the time (highest) and refused malicious ones 79.8% (lowest). The blocking classifier is the primary harm-prevention mechanism.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: Opus 5.5 itself rarely refuses legitimate security work. Any friction on audit sessions will come from classifier rerouting, not model refusals.

gapFacts.claim: The alignment section lists the fallback targets as Opus 4.8 for cyber content and Opus 5 for biology and AI R&D content.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the AI R&D fallback goes to Opus 5, so it matters for our infra/agent-tooling work only at the frontier-LLM margin, and it costs at most a step down to our incumbent.

gapFacts.claim: The announcement says distillation safeguards fall back to another model. This contradicts the system card (p.13) and the API docs, which say distillation/reasoning_extraction blocks have no fallback and are not retried.
gapFacts.impl: Source conflict. Trust the card and docs (no fallback) for judge/verifier prompts. Do not rely on a retry.

gapFacts.claim: The card's cyber capability results were run with cyber safeguards OFF via the API. Several sections likewise disable production safeguards, so capability numbers may not describe the deployed, rerouting system.
gapFacts.impl: Check each section's stated configuration before using a number as a deployed-fleet estimate.

gapFacts.claim: Cyber Verification Program is the recommended route for security use cases blocked by cyber safeguards. Opus 5.5 is not yet in it.
On TB4, Opus 5.5 at xhigh (66.36%) is within noise of max (64.8%). It ran in Claude Code --bare mode; comparators ran at max effort.

Where max is needed, Fable 5.1 at max spends fewer output tokens (it also draws down Fable's separate sub-cap faster). [VERIFIER: 'Opus 5.5 max is the most token-hungry Claude point' is correct. And 'Fable's separate sub-cap' is not in the source. The operator's own policy says Fable is a sub-cap of the SAME weekly bucket, not a separate budget.]

gapFacts.claim: CursorBench 4.0 cost per task: Opus 5.5 is about 0.24x Opus 5 at low, 0.42x at medium, 0.44x at high and 0.61x at xhigh, but about 1.12x at max.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: a second independent harness (Cursor) shows the same crossover between xhigh and max. Because Opus 5.5's per-token prices are 0.8x, the implied token ratio is higher than the cost ratio (about 1.4x at max). Quota-wise, max on Opus 5.5 is not cheaper than Opus 5 at max. [VERIFIER: 'About 1.4x tokens at max' assumes a uniform 0.8x price ratio. Only uncached input and output are 20% cheaper; cache reads are $0.20 vs Opus 5's $0.50, 60% less (announce L31), and they 'make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs'. So the implied token ratio at max is higher than 1.4x and cannot be pinned down without the token mix. Opus 5 costs are also Cursor's published figures, not Anthropic's list-price computation, so the two arms may not be priced the same way. The crossover observation itself is sound.]

gapFacts.claim: AutomationBench (Zapier) cost per task: Opus 5.5 is 0.67x to 0.75x Opus 5 from low through xhigh and 1.08x at max, while scoring higher at every level.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: this is the third per-task source where Opus 5.5 costs more than Opus 5 only at max. The gap is smaller on tool-heavy API workflows, where cached input tokens dominate. [VERIFIER: 'Third source where Opus 5.5 costs more only at max' is supported (FrontierCode tokens, CursorBench, AutomationBench). The explanation 'where cached input tokens dominate' is not in the source; no token mix is given for AutomationBench. Also, the two arms are costed by different parties (Anthropic's calculation vs Zapier's leaderboard), which the caption states.]

gapFacts.claim: Docs: at the same effort, Opus 5.5 thinks more per turn than Opus 5, especially at xhigh and max. A user who keeps the Opus 5 effort value should expect longer turns and more output tokens. No figure is given.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: per-turn and per-task disagree below xhigh (fewer tokens per task). Per-turn size, not per-task spend, is what max_tokens bounds, so size max_tokens up even where per-task quota falls.

gapFacts.claim: What's-new page: more thinking per turn at a given effort, most of all at xhigh and max. It says to re-run the effort sweep rather than carry a setting over, and to leave room in max_tokens.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: vendor guidance explicitly says Opus 5 effort settings do not carry over. Our fleet's effort mapping must be re-derived, not copied.

gapFacts.claim: Effort names do not map to the same amount of thinking across models. Opus 5.5 at medium matches or exceeds Opus 5 at high on coding and knowledge work, and at low it comes close to Opus 5 at high on several coding evals at much lower cost.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the equivalent of our Opus 5 at high default is Opus 5.5 at medium (or low for some coding work), not Opus 5.5 at high.

gapFacts.claim: On the max_tokens budget: thinking counts toward max_tokens even when not returned. For long agentic coding turns Anthropic found max_tokens of 128,000, the model maximum, worked well. A limit sized for Opus 5 with thinking off can cut replies off.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: for API/Workflow agents on Opus 5.5 at high and above, set max_tokens to 128k. This differs from the 64k starting point that applied to Opus 5 (g2#F14).

gapFacts.claim: Docs' max_tokens starting point for Opus 5 at xhigh or max is 64k tokens. Opus 5.5 keeps Opus 5's 1M context and 128k max output.
gapFacts.n: Opus 5: start 64k; Opus 5.5: 128k recommended; both 128k max output, 1M context
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the vendor's own starting max_tokens doubles from Opus 5 (64k) to Opus 5.5 (128k), which is consistent with bigger per-turn thinking at high effort. The output ceiling is unchanged at 128k.

gapFacts.claim: Opus 5.5 defaults to medium effort while Opus 5 defaulted to high, so a request that omits effort runs one level lower on Opus 5.5.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: the '40% cheaper at default settings' claims compare Opus 5.5 at medium with Opus 5 at high. Our launcher's explicit '--effort high' would forfeit part of that saving.

gapFacts.claim: Guide: the model finishes the same task with fewer tokens. At default medium it matched or beat Opus 5 at high on multistep repository work in fewer steps and with fewer tokens.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: 'more per turn' and 'fewer per task' fit together only if turns per task drop a lot. No source quantifies turns per task, so the per-turn multiplier cannot be derived. [VERIFIER: 'No source quantifies turns per task' is false. p.211 Table 8.14.5.A gives Toolathlon average assistant turns per trajectory at max effort: Opus 5.5 26.9 vs Opus 5 23.5, so MORE turns. announce L212 (Optiver) says 'about half the turns'. L228 (Kiro) says 'about 40% fewer calls'. L188 (Lovable) says 'a third to half fewer steps'. Also, L39 compares DIFFERENT levels (5.5 medium vs 5 high), which needs no turn reduction to fit the same-level 'more per turn' claim. The tension exists only at matched level (the FrontierCode data).]

gapFacts.claim: Guide on low effort: at low the model keeps its thinking short, and how often it skips thinking entirely depends on the prompt. Separately, follow-up requests that only process tool results can skip thinking at any level.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: low-effort Opus 5.5 is the replacement for Opus 5 runs with thinking disabled (mechanical edits, retrieval). Per-turn cost there is small but must be measured.

gapFacts.claim: CoT controllability chart (Fig 6.6.4.4.A; GPQA/HLE/MMLU-Pro Q&A): mean CoT length for Opus 5.5 at four unlabeled settings. The top setting thinks about 15-17x the third, and about 31-33x the lowest. Opus 5 is not on the chart.

On short Q&A the lower settings think under ~800 chars, so thinking cost is concentrated at the top setting. No Opus 5 per-turn comparison can be drawn.

gapFacts.claim: In the within-model knowledge-work data, xhigh matches max while using about 51% (GDPval-AA) and 41% (AA-Briefcase) fewer output tokens.

gapFacts.claim: Announcement: Opus 5.5 uses fewer tokens per task than Opus 5, which with lower per-token prices nets out to about 40% lower cost. At default settings it costs 40% less on typical workloads.

The same line L31 says cache reads are 60% cheaper and make up the majority of agentic/coding costs, so a 40% cost cut is consistent with roughly flat or even higher total token volume. The token reduction cannot be backed out from the headline 40%.]

gapFacts.claim: Early-tester token claims versus Opus 5 (efforts mostly unstated): Box ~1/3 of the tokens; Kiro half the tokens and ~40% fewer calls; Optiver ~half the turns and output tokens; the codebase-audit tester had Opus 5 use 2.5x as many tokens.

That is the only turn-normalisable data point, and it is anecdotal. [VERIFIER: The Optiver arithmetic (per-turn output roughly at parity) is fine. 'The only turn-normalisable data point' is wrong. gapFacts.claim: On ProgramBench, the 5-agent team reached a 0.6 score with about 2.7x less latency than the single agent. Async subagents fell in between.
gapFacts.n: approx. time to 0.6: team ~2,200 s, async ~4,000 s, single ~6,000 s; all converge ~0.97
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: The 2.7x speedup describes agents at an unstated effort, probably max. It does not show that low- or medium-effort teammates keep the same speedup.

gapFacts.claim: Teams spend more tokens for the same score. In the ProgramBench score-vs-tokens chart the single agent is most token-efficient: about 0.6 at ~0.55M tokens, against ~1.1M for the 5-agent team and ~2M for async subagents.
gapFacts.n: approx. tokens to 0.6: single ~0.55M, 5-team ~1.1M, async ~2M; single ~0.85 at ~1M; async curve extends to ~60M
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: Under a quota binding, a 5-agent team costs roughly 2x the tokens of a single agent for the same score. Buy that only when wall-clock matters. [VERIFIER: The '~2x' ratio depends on score. At ~0.9 it is ~1.4M vs ~2.3M (~1.6x), and team and single converge near 0.95. Below ~0.3, async subagents sit ABOVE the single agent (more token-efficient). §8.12.5 also counts tokens per context window, summed across agents ('every token that enters an agent's context window ... counted once per window rather than once per model request'). That is not billed quota, so quota cost cannot be read off this axis directly.]

gapFacts.claim: Multi-agent DRACO: at a 0.5x latency budget the 5-agent team more than matched single-agent performance with a roughly 2.8x speedup (max effort).

gapFacts.claim: Reducing effort and tightening a latency budget both cut latency but work differently: lower effort does less work, while a budget keeps more work by sustaining parallelism.
gapFacts.impl: INFERENCE: This is the card's only qualitative statement on effort for teams, and it is not measured. No figure plots team score against effort.

gapFacts.claim: Knowledge-base score for Opus 5.5 within 2, 6 and 24 hours, by team size (1/10/30/100).

gapFacts.claim: Lean score for Opus 5.5 within 2, 6 and 24 hours, by team size (1/10/30/100).

critic.coverage_verdict: Coverage is near-complete. All 221 capability, safety and alignment pages and all six web pages were read. I checked the TOC: the only unread pages are the appendix (pp.222-230: welfare interview questions and the HLE blocklist), which has nothing on utilization. What remains is mostly synthesis, not re-reading. (1) The benign-coding fallback rates are already in the facts: 2.5-3.9% of requests on TB4.0 and TB-Science, and 1 of 324 trials on Toolathlon. (2) The FrontierCode token-per-effort data already answers 'thinks more per turn': Opus 5.5 uses fewer tokens per task than Opus 5 from low to high and about 1.5x more at max. (3) Under the p.174 caption, the unlabeled-effort ProgramBench, SWE-bench and team runs default to max. The decision-critical unknowns cannot be answered from these sources: weekly-quota accounting, Claude Code's default effort, per-effort alignment rates, mixed-model or low-effort teams, and long-context degradation. They should be reported as NOT STATED and settled by our own effort sweeps.

gaps.question: How often does ordinary (non-security) agentic coding traffic get rerouted by a safeguard to a weaker model, and how much does that change the served mix for coding teammates and code-review or audit sessions?
gaps.where: No re-read is needed; these facts are already in the base but were never put together. System card p.178 (TB4.0: 2.5% of requests, 10% of trials), p.179 (TB-Science: 3.9% of requests, 5% of trials), p.210 (Toolathlon: 1 of 324 trials stopped by a classifier), p.57 Fig 3.4.2.A (4.5% flag rate on defensive vulnerability-discovery traffic), and pp.86-88 (Gray Swan: 46% of coding rollouts served by Opus 4.8; adaptive coding eval: 64%). The fallback model is named on p.12 (cyber goes to Opus 4.8; bio and frontier-LLM go to Opus 5). The TB4 and TB-Science pages do not say which category fired.
gaps.why: The c6 and c7 readers listed 'no false-positive or fallback rate on ordinary coding traffic' as absent, but the benchmark-side rates exist. That decides whether security-audit and review workloads should run on Opus 5.5 at all: the security-adjacent share is served by Opus 4.8, and every successful coding-injection attack came through that fallback. The adversarial rates (46% and 64%) must be kept separate from the benign-task rates (2.5-3.9% of requests).

gaps.question: At the same effort level, how many more (or fewer) tokens does Opus 5.5 spend than Opus 5, per task and per turn? This sets max_tokens headroom and whether an Opus 5 effort setting can be carried over.
gaps.where: System card p.176 Fig 8.4.A and p.177 Fig 8.4.B already give output tokens per task at each effort for both models (already in the base as c1#F9/F10/F12). Also re-read p.150 Fig 6.6.4.4.A (image /tmp/opus55-src/figs/fig-150-070.png): it plots mean chain-of-thought length for Opus 5.5 at 4 unlabeled settings (~400, ~550, ~750, ~12.5k chars) against Opus 4.8 and Mythos 5.1. Opus 5 is not on that chart.
gaps.why: c9 lists 'no figure for how much more Opus 5.5 thinks per turn' as absent, and prompting.txt L48 says only 'thinks more per turn'. The FrontierCode data answers the per-task question. Opus 5.5 uses far fewer output tokens than Opus 5 at low, medium and high (~9k vs 23k, 17.5k vs 33k, 26k vs 58k), about the same at xhigh (~60k vs 62k), and about 1.5x more at max (~155k vs 100k). So an effort value carried over from Opus 5 saves quota only up to high and costs more at max. That changes the lead and teammate effort choice. The p.150 chart adds a within-model reading: roughly a 30x jump between Opus 5.5's third and fourth settings.

gaps.question: At what effort were the single-agent ProgramBench, SWE-bench, DeepSWE, multi-agent ProgramBench and large-team (1/10/30/100 agent) runs made?
gaps.where: System card p.174, Table 8.1.A caption: 'Unless otherwise noted, all Claude Opus 5.5 results use ... adaptive thinking at max effort ... averaged over five trials'. §8.12.1 (p.189) and §8.12.3 (p.193) give no other effort. Only multi-agent DRACO states max explicitly (p.193).
gaps.why: The c1 and c2 readers recorded these as 'effort not stated'. Under the p.174 default they are max-effort results. So every team-size and speedup finding (the 2.7x and 2.8x speedups, the team scaling curves) describes max-effort agents, and says nothing about low- or medium-effort teammates, which is the configuration a quota-bound fleet would run. The large-team and multi-agent runs used a different snapshot, so this default is an inference, not a direct statement.
